title: Owned or Borrowed?

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Return a borrow when the result is a view into an input; return an owned value when new data is created or must escape independently. The choice affects allocation and API flexibility.

The lifetime of the data behind a return value should determine its type. `trimmed(input: &str) -> &str` returns a view into existing bytes, so it can avoid allocation, but the caller cannot keep the result after the input is gone. `label(input: &str) -> String` creates uppercase text in a new owned buffer. The caller may keep that buffer independently of the input. Neither choice is universally better; each promises a different relationship.

Follow the example with a `String` created in an inner block. A borrowed trimmed view must be used before the source leaves the block. An owned uppercase result can be moved out and printed afterward. If a function sometimes borrows and sometimes must allocate, `std::borrow::Cow<'a, str>` can express either case, but it adds complexity that a beginner API may not need. First choose a clear owned or borrowed contract, then optimize if measurements justify it.

Do not return a reference to a local `String` assembled inside a function; the value would be dropped when the function returns. Return that `String` by value instead, relying on move semantics. Conversely, do not allocate just to return a substring that the caller will use briefly while the input remains alive. Test both signatures with a string literal and with an owned string. Ask who owns the bytes after the call and how long the result must remain valid; those answers should make the return type feel inevitable.

A borrowed return can still be ergonomic: callers can call `.to_owned()` only when they need independence. That lets the common short-lived path avoid allocation while preserving an explicit escape hatch.
writing.question: Why does label return `String`?
writing.rule: Return a borrow when the result is a view into an input; return an owned value when new data is created or must escape independently.
writing.success: You can say which result can outlive `input`, and why each return type fits its body.
